stories.title: Denmark slams 'reckless' firing of flares by Russian ship
stories.summary: Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen has condemned as "reckless" a Russian frigate firing flares at a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea yesterday. The armed forces said in a statement last night that "one of the air force's Fennec helicopters was fired at with flares during a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate, which was located in international waters off Gedser," Denmark's southernmost town. The Russian ship had fired "two flares towards the helicopter. One of the flares passed at close range to the helicopter," it added. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen slammed the incident as "reckless action from Russia". "Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver," Ms Frederiksen said in a statement on X. PM Mette Frederiksen: "Reckless action from Russia towards Danish military during a routine overflight yesterday. Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver."

stories.title: Distilleries cautiously welcome Trump tariff announcement
stories.summary: A distillery in Co Longford has given a cautious welcome after US President Donald Trump said he will lift tariffs on imports of Irish whiskey. Mr Trump used his speech yesterday at the Irish Open golf tournament in Doonbeg, Co Clare to announce he is to remove the tariffs. He told the crowd who had congregated on the 18th green that he had spoken with Taoiseach Micheál Martin and Irish Open winner Shane Lowry about US tariffs on Irish whiskey. Lough Ree Distillery founder Michael Clancy said: "I think we cautiously welcome it but the proof of the pudding is in the eating. "We hope it will happen and I was listening to Olaf Gill earlier and he said there are a lot of products on the list that they would like to see tariffs lifted from," he added. Mr Clancy explained that even though they are only a small producer, they have been impacted by the 10% tariffs on Irish whiskey.

stories.title: Burnham will be last Prime Minister of UK, says Swinney
stories.summary: Andy Burnham will be the last Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, Scottish First Minister John Swinney has predicted. The SNP leader said a Scottish independence referendum should happen within the next five years. Mr Swinney spoke at a joint press conference with the leaders of Sinn Féin and Plaid Cymru where they jointly declared that "Westminster's time is coming to an end". The devolved leaders are seeking to pressure Andy Burnham into agreeing to hold independence referendums. Mr Swinney, along with Sinn Féin vice president Michelle O’Neill and Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth, signed the memorandum of understanding during a meeting in Cardiff in Wales this morning. Along with Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald, the leaders said each has "the right to self-determination" and called for the UK government to "prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change in each jurisdiction".

stories.title: Oil rises above $108 on attacks and pipeline outage
stories.summary: Oil prices rose more than 2% today after attacks on Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure left the kingdom's East-West pipeline offline, raising fears that damage to energy infrastructure and transport routes could take longer to repair. Brent crude futures rose $2.5, or 2.37%, to $108.18 a barrel this morning, while US West Texas Intermediate futures were up $2.46, or 2.43%, at $103.85 a barrel. Concerns over oil supplies intensified after Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen launched fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia yesterday, while Gulf Arab states postponed planned discussions with Iran. "Fresh attacks by the Houthis targeting Saudi Arabia may be influencing oil market investors' expectations about the severity and duration of the conflict," said Hamad Hussain, senior climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics. The Houthis said they fired dozens of missiles and drones at a military airbase in Khamis Mushait in southern Saudi Arabia, targeting aircraft hangars, radar systems, runways and ammunition depots in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen. This followed attacks on Friday on Saudi Arabia, which Riyadh blamed on Iranian-backed fighters in Iraq, that disrupted the country's East-West pipeline, which allows oil exports to bypass the blockaded Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of global oil supplies previously passed.

stories.summary: US President Donald Trump said that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other's energy facilities, a day after he chastised Ukraine for hitting Russian oil refineries. "Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do so, likewise! The World's Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran," Mr Trump said on his Truth Social network. In response, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine is ready to halt strikes on Russia if its partners ensure that ⁠Russia will refrain from hitting Ukrainian energy facilities, infrastructure and food supply routes. Mr Zelensky added that Ukraine was not convinced that Russia was willing to abide by any agreement. "The ‌war must be brought to an end. And a de-escalatory step regarding critical ⁠infrastructure could be the first step ‌toward peace. We expect specifics from our partners," he said in a post on X. Earlier, the EU's top diplomat said that Russian strikes which hit a Warsaw-bound train near Ukraine's border with Poland shortly after top Western figures passed through were meant to "scare" off Ukraine's backers.

stories.title: Controversial Sweeney ad is outdated and silly - Duggan
stories.summary: Former Republic of Ireland international footballer Karen Duggan believes the backlash to a controversial advert featuring actor Sydney Sweeney has "flipped the script in a positive way", and put more focus on the commitment it takes to be a successful female athlete. Sweeney’s new advert for American betting company Novig, in which she wears little to no clothing and is covered with sports equipment, has received significant criticism from the female sporting community. Australian four-time Olympic swimmer Ariarne Titmus, American gymnast Gracie Kramer and English sprinter Amy Hunt are among those who have spoken out about it, with Hunt airing her concern the ad could become a "barrier" to young girls wanting to play sport. However Duggan said the positivity of women in sport speaking out against the advert has already overtaken any negative impact. "I think it uses an outdated formula of, you know, attractive women, sports imagery, and a bit of controversy to sell a product. I don't think it was ever intended to represent female athletes or women in sport or the reality of that. "My biggest criticism of it is that I don't think women were part of that conversation at all.

stories.title: Antrim clubs await fate as violence mars hurling clash
stories.summary: Antrim clubs Loughgiel and St John's will await their fate after violent scenes marred their senior hurling clash at Fr Healy Park. The group encounter, a repeat of last year’s county final, passed off without any major incident over the course of 63 minutes, with reigning champions St John’s losing out 3-14 to 0-30. Both sides advanced to the knockout stages in a game that saw just three yellow cards handed out. At the full-time whistle however tempers flared between both panels. Initially players and mentors on both sides clashed in the middle of the pitch, before footage from the ground shows how things escalated further with the violence spilling over into the crowd. The clubs will now await any proposed penalties resulting from the action.

stories.title: Tielemans frustrated by United's derby defeat display
stories.summary: Youri Tielemans expressed frustration with Manchester United's meek performance in the controversial derby defeat to 10-man Manchester City. Michael Carrick’s men have made a sluggish start to the Premier League season, with a humiliating defeat at Hull, victory against Ipswich and late draw at Everton followed by derby disappointment on Sunday. Phil Foden was sent off for kicking out at Bruno Fernandes midway through the first half but United failed to take advantage, with Erling Haaland’s contentious effort eventually sealing a 1-0 win for City. Pro Ref, the refereeing body, would contact the Red Devils that evening to acknowledge an "error in judgement" in overturning the offside call rather than sending referee Michael Oliver for an on-field review given Enzo Fernandez was interfering with play. United’s fury at the officiating for that decision is as clear as it is understandable, but summer signing Tielemans admits they were not good enough regardless of that moment. "It’s disappointing, so everyone is disappointed and frustrated because we know we can play so much better," the Belgium international told MUTV.

stories.title: O'Dowd determined to nail down starting shirt once again
stories.summary: Ireland prop Niamh O'Dowd is determined to win back the starting loosehead jersey in the upcoming test window, but knows that Ireland's strength in depth makes it a difficult task. Ireland will play five games across September and October, four of which under the WXV Global Series umbrella, with many viewing the block as a chance for Scott Bemand to blood new options, and to rotate his squad. One such player who will be keen to put their hand up is Wexford's Niamh O'Dowd, who has had a mixed past two years in green. Having played in nine of Ireland's 11 tests in 2025, including three World Cup starts, O'Dowd has had to settle for just three bench appearances in the Six Nations so far in 2026. Nonetheless, O'Dowd enjoyed the experience of providing some boom from the bomb squad. "Like you know (that) if you come on at 50, 55 minutes, it's like a really exciting time of a game and it's kind of all in the balance sometimes at that stage. So I think if you kind of change your perspective on it.

stories.title: Filmmakers D.A.D.D.Y. take over RTÉ Culture for Culture Night
stories.summary: Writer/directors Mike Ahern and Enda Loughman, known collectively as D.A.D.D.Y. (Design, Animation, Design, Design, Yay!), have spent over two decades crafting distinctive work across commercials, music videos, television and film. Their work is defined by a love of comedy, big cinematic ideas, small details, and stories filled with warmth and weirdness. Their debut feature film, Extra Ordinary, starring Maeve Higgins and Will Forte, premiered in competition at the SXSW festival and went on to win awards and rave reviews. Recently, they directed episodes of Chris O'Dowd’s TV series Small Town, Big Story, starring Christina Hendricks and Paddy Considine. Their current slate includes a serialised adaptation of Extra Ordinary, the animated series Beasts of Burden for Netflix, and new film projects with Skydance, Aardman, and Lord & Miller. D.A.D.D.Y. duo Enda Loughman (L) and Mike Ahern (R) plus unnamed friends \u003Cp\u003EWill Forte and Maeve Higgins in Extra Ordinary\u003C/p\u003E

stories.title: Oasis to play two nights at Slane Castle next September
stories.summary: Oasis have announced that they will play Slane Castle on the 4 and 5 of September 2027 with registration to buy tickets open now. The Slane dates are part of the band's new 38-date world tour which will also see them play concerts in the UK, Europe and the US, including five nights at Celtic Park in Glasgow, 11 nights at Etihad Stadium in Manchester, and four nights at Kenbworth. Fans can register to buy tickets here, with a warning that they must register before Thursday 17 September 4pm BST for a chance to buy tickets. In a statement, Oasis said: "Start the celebrations. After a period of reflection 'The Most Damaging Pop Cultural Force In Recent British History' has declared itself fit for purpose and will once again return to lift the spirits of the people. In an effort to avoid a repeat of the confusion and outcry over ticket sales for the band's last tour, strict new rules have been introduced. Fans are asked to register to secure their tickets, with standard ticket prices fixed between €181.25 to €501.25. Tickets are limited to four per person.

stories.title: Wexford student makes his Debs waistcoat from curtains
stories.summary: On 24 August, Vinnie Doyle Roche and his good friend Tegan walked into the Bunclody Debs in Wexford, looking exceptionally stylish. The two had decided weeks in advance what their colour scheme would be, but hadn't managed to actually buy anything for the big event. Two weeks out, Tegan was ready to go, but Vinnie found himself without a suit or waistcoat. After searching high and low for the right shade of green, he found a suit in Murt Walsh Menswear in Gorey. "I had wanted to make my own waistcoat anyway because we do a sewing class on a Wednesday in the Community Care in Carnew," he explained. Vinnie's grandmother, Florence Roche, and his mum are both keen sewers. So between the crafty family and Miriam, the woman who runs the community sewing class, the debutant was in good hands. "When I was telling people I was going to make it myself, they were all very interested to see how it would turn out," he admits. "At this point, I hadn't even any material for it or anything."

stories.summary: Iran's security chief has rejected any talks with the United States after President Donald Trump said he was open to resuming discussions on the Middle East war. "Don't get distracted by the US president's mixed signals - from 'no negotiations' to 'we're ready to talk'," the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, posted on X. stories.title: Increase in vehicle, farm crime over six years - CSO
stories.summary: Personal, household, vehicle, and farm crime have increased over the past six years according to the latest Crime and Victimisation report for 2025. The Central Statistics Office (CSO) has published the results of a household survey about crime in Ireland. Respondents were asked to consider the previous 12 months and rate how crime had impacted their lives and how effectively it had been dealt with by the justice system. In 2025, 19% of respondents said they had been a victim of some form of personal crime compared with 10% in 2019. Personal crime includes violent and non-violent theft, fraud, and physical assault. More than one in ten people were victims of fraud last year compared with 4% in 2019, with card payment fraud accounting for almost half of such crimes.

stories.title: Tóibín targets dozen Aontú seats, rules out FG coalition
stories.summary: Aontú leader Peadar Tóibín has told his party's think-in that it is targeting up to a dozen seats in the next Dáil election. Speaking at the event in Co Derry this morning, Mr Tóibín referenced recent polling which put his party at 8% of the vote. He said that could translate into a decent number of seats at the next election. He told delegates that a dozen seats was not impossible "on a good day", and that Aontú had very strong chances in constituencies like Cavan/Monaghan, Meath East, Dublin West, Wexford and Limerick City. He said he believed the party's strong showing at the polls was happening because it was "listening to the people" and that others had lost touch with their base. He ruled out going into government with Fine Gael after the next election and while he said they would "find it very difficult to put Micheál Martin back into power", the likelihood was that he might have been replaced by his party by then.

stories.title: All you need to know about plug-in solar panels for your home
stories.summary: Analysis: These panels can be plugged into a standard wall socket to generate solar power from a balcony, shed roof or any other outdoor space Imagine a device that you plug into a normal household socket which generates rather than uses electricity so you can use it anywhere in your home. This is a reality today for over a million homeowners across Germany (and more recently in the UK) and hopefully will be in Ireland sometime soon. The device I am talking about is plug-in solar (sometimes called balcony solar), as it is used by many apartment owners in Germany on their balconies to make their own electricity from sunlight. Firstly, it's important to state that this technology is not a 'game changer' or a 'no-brainer' and it is not going to radically lower anyone's electricity bill. However, if used well and in specific situations, it can make a helpful reduction to someone's electricity bills. The system typically consists of a solar panel(s), a power cable, a box with some electronics inside called an inverter and a regular plug. From Euronews, how Germans are using balcony solar to fight climate change and high energy bills It works like regular solar panel systems which we now see on almost 200,000 homes and business in Ireland, but at a much smaller scale. A typical set-up for conventional solar panels on a house might have anything from four to 20 panels on a roof, whereas these 'plug-in' systems are smaller, typically one or two panels. The way it works is that you place the solar panel outside in your garden or on your balcony and the cable from the solar panel passes into your house and is plugged into a regular socket (unless you have an outside weatherproof socket). Within the system, there are some electronics that cleverly change the electricity produced by the solar panel to the same technical characteristics as the electricity inside your home coming from the power grid. This makes the electricity coming from the system look and feel like regular electricity for your appliances in the house.

stories.title: Canada seeks 'unique alliance' with EU, but not to join
stories.summary: Canada is seeking a "unique alliance" with the European Union but is ⁠not looking to become a member, Prime Minister Mark Carney has said. It comes after the Wall Street Journal reported he was exploring whether Canada could become an "associate member" of the bloc. The EU, which has not been flexible about membership rules in the past, is open to the idea of granting Canada a yet-to-be-created status of associate membership, the newspaper reported, citing unnamed officials both from the EU and Canada. "We're not looking to become a member of the European Union," Mr Carney said. "What we are looking - and will begin discussions for - is a unique alliance between Canada and the European Union," he told reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival. "We share the same values, we have the same priorities and we have very complementary strengths."

stories.title: No credit in the bank for McGuinness after Kerry slaying
stories.summary: Would he or would he not? In the end, we found out this week that he would. Jim McGuinness has taken up the option of a fourth year in charge of Donegal, in this his second term as manager of the county's senior footballers. Perhaps it is no surprise, given that he will want to atone for how 2026 ended. In many ways Donegal's exit from the championship was somewhat bizarre on the year's longest day. The sun may have been at its highest overlooking Croke Park, but Donegal were deriving little energy from its rays despite taking Dublin to extra-time. It was clear to see that McGuinness's men were finding it a bit of a churn, though credit to them for forcing the additional periods after Michael Murphy nailed a late two-pointer. But it was just delaying the inevitable as the Dubs won with a bit to spare. The camera honed in on Murphy and the question of whether he'll grace the Jones's Road sod again was percolating. Still no word on the 37-year-old's Tír Chonaill future. After what Donegal had done for much of the previous six months, it may not be too hyperbolic to say that their championship exit bordered on the unbelievable - and we are not trying to go all Charlie Haughey GUBU here!

stories.title: Saudi football body vows action over Jota chants
stories.summary: Saudi Arabian football authorities have promised to take action and Cristiano Ronaldo has called for life bans after rival fans taunted Al-Hilal's Ruben Neves about the death of Diogo Jota, his friend and former Portugal team-mate. Chants about Jota, the Liverpool and Portugal forward who died in a car crash last year, rang out during Al-Hilal's 6-0 away win over Al-Taawoun on Saturday. "The league must take action and punish this kind of fan behaviour," Saudi-based Portugal captain Ronaldo wrote on Instagram on Sunday. "People who behave like this should never be allowed to enter a stadium again," he added. Midfielder Neves, 29, reacted to the chants coming from the stands by sarcastically giving a thumbs-up and applauding, before pointing towards the sky. "I just hope they don't go to pray later after what they did," he said after the match.

stories.summary: In a sport where bland personalities often tend to get rewarded, women's rugby provides the necessary antidote as prescribed for the soul. The Irish team are a shining light of this theory. Despite hitting real doldrum times in the early part of this decade, the women's game has never been healthier on the island; powered by the personalities in green who show up on and off the field. The biggest names in the online space are arguably Anna McGann and Eve Higgins. Between them, the pair have amassed over 35,000 followers on TikTok, 29,000 on Instagram; plus more than 1.1 million likes on their videos on the former app. Yet, when asked how they rose to prominence, there was a shared look, a cheeky grin and a typically humble Irish response. She added: "No, literally, we were just away at the World Cup rooming together for three and a half weeks so we had to come up with things to keep us busy. "And yeah, we just made a TikTok of the viral Canterbury Fleece and people wanted it and they couldn't get their hands on it. So they wanted it even more and that's kind of where it began from.

stories.title: Sebastian Barry's bold new novel crosses the American frontier
stories.summary: By now, the Irish fascination with the American frontier could almost be classed as its own genre. From Rory Gallagher's Out on the Western Plain to Kevin Barry’s The Heart in Winter, something about the expansiveness of the West must speak to an innately Irish sense of yearning. Perhaps it has to do with the centuries of oppression which Irish people experienced under the yoke of British colonialism. Perhaps it finds its roots in the waves of emigration which started during the Famine and continue to this day. "… Every Irish person was an expert on [starvation]," as Sebastian Barry’s protagonist puts it in his latest novel The Newer World. "About that he said nothing more." Nevertheless, we know that when our ancestors first started landing on American shores, their dreams of a better life didn’t always materialise. During the 1860s, for example, Irish men were drafted by their thousands – often just after their ships had docked – and sent off to die in a civil war they couldn’t possibly have known anything about. By now, the Irish fascination with the American frontier could almost be classed as its own genre. Harsh as this treatment of Irish people was, it pales in comparison to the transatlantic slave trade, over which the American Civil War was fought and which is estimated to have enslaved around 12.5 million people over three centuries. It’s against this backdrop that The Newer World takes place, following the travails of freed slave Tennyson Bouguereau as he tries to survive the so-called Reconstruction era in post-War Tennessee.

stories.title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran's US tour
stories.summary: US rapper Macklemore has been dropped from the remaining dates of Ed Sheeran's US tour following controversy over comments he made in support of Palestine during a concert in New Jersey. Macklemore, whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty, spoke in support of people in Gaza and the West Bank while performing at the MetLife Stadium earlier this month. In a statement to Rolling Stone, Messina Touring Group, promoter of the US leg of Sheeran’s Loop Tour, confirmed that Macklemore would not perform on the remaining support dates. The promoter said it had been notified by venues hosting upcoming dates that they would not allow concerts to take place with Macklemore on the line-up. It said this would result in the cancellation of the tour and affect hundreds of thousands of fans. stories.title: Toyota previews the new Hilux at the Ploughing
stories.summary: Toyota's Hilux may be around for the last 70 years, but its basic purpose hasn’t changed. It is made to be a functional load-carrying workhorse with Four Wheel Drive capability for those who need substance over style. The latest version of the double cab Hilux to arrive here has gone on view at the National Ploughing Championships. It has had various styling tweaks inspired by the Land Cruiser - pronounced lines and flanks, a new honeycomb grille and slim new headlights - yet the dimensions remain essentially the same as the older model in terms of length, height and width. The entry-level version starts at €44,234, excluding VAT, and it gets some interesting kit as standard. Adaptive cruise control, a 12.3" infotainment screen, electric steering and a heated steering wheel are all standard, and the padding and upholstery in the front seats has been strengthened and improved. The Hilux is also Apple and Android enabled and has wireless phone charging. The engine is the familiar 2.8 diesel, and there’s a mild-hybrid functionality. Toyota claims an average fuel consumption figure of 9.7 litres of diesel per 100 kilometres.

stories.title: EU to outline curbs on children accessing social media
stories.summary: Children and teenagers aged under 15 will not be able to open a social media account without express parental or guardian permission, while those aged under 13 will only be able to access "child friendly" alternatives, under new draft plans set to be outlined by the European Commission president. Ursula von der Leyen's proposal, expected to be called 'EU Kids Act', will be outlined in her annual state of the union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg tomorrow. It will then be further detailed on Thursday by Ms von der Leyen and her colleague Henna Virkkunen, who is the EU's executive vice-president of tech sovereignty, security and democracy. The draft plans are expected to include what is being termed a "block" or "delay" on children and teenagers' access to social media platforms. While a specific age restriction has not yet been finalised, it is expected the draft plan will include four stages: The Irish Government and its counterparts in other EU member states have in recent months emphasised the need for some kind of social media restrictions to be introduced for children and young teens, with an under-16s ban previously mooted.

stories.title: Andrews responds to Trump's united Ireland comments
stories.summary: A Fianna Fáil MEP has responded to US President Donald Trump's intervention in the united Ireland debate by saying: "Mr Trump has decided to get involved, what could possibly go wrong". Barry Andrews made the comments during a European Parliament discussion in Strasbourg, France, this evening. Speaking during a one-minute speeches debate on a series of different topics in the parliament, Mr Andrews referenced Mr Trump's comments about a united Ireland during his visit to the Irish Open at the weekend. The Fianna Fáil MEP who has previously criticised the US president's time in power, responded dryly, "Mr Trump has decided to get involved in the debate on a united Ireland, what could possibly go wrong? As [SDLP MP] Claire Hanna has said, he's perhaps not as orange as he looks." "People who take Ireland's future seriously don't take Trump's comments seriously," he added. Mr Andrews continued by referencing new British prime minister Andy Burnham's recent comments that a united Ireland referendum is for now "off the table" as it is not believed by Downing Street that the majority of people currently want a referendum.

stories.title: Trump unity remarks reflect broad US sentiment - Adams
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump's remarks in support of Irish unity reflect the "broad north American sentiment", former Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams has said. Mr Adams welcomed Mr Trump's remarks but stated that Taoiseach Micheál Martin had "put himself outside this positive attitude" towards holding a border poll. The US president is currently on a two-day visit to Ireland. Yesterday, during a meeting with Mr Martin, Mr Trump claimed Irish reunification was inevitable, adding it "may as well happen now". "But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?" During a subsequent engagement at the US Ambassador's residence in Ireland, Mr Trump did not back away from his earlier answer, stating Irish unification would be "a very cool thing". Mr Adams, who was the Sinn Féin leader when the Good Friday Agreement was signed in 1998, delivered a speech in Dublin today reflecting on the peace deal.

stories.title: ESB Group's half year profits up 20% to €377m
stories.summary: ESB has reported profits after tax of €377m for the six months to the end of June, a 20% increase on profits of €313m the same time last year, when the company had been impacted by costs in its networks business due to Storm Éowyn. It noted that profits in its Customer Solutions division - which includes its retail brands like Electric Ireland - fell by €10m, while Generation Trading profits increased by €22m as both units were impacted by renewed energy price volatility due to the conflict in the Middle East. The company said that the conflict in the Middle East, and ongoing global geopolitical instability, has created upward pressure on wholesale gas and oil prices, particularly from February onwards. Because of this Electric Ireland increased its electricity and gas prices from July of this year - the first time it had increased prices since October 2022. The company said today that despite the challenge of ongoing volatility, Electric Ireland residential electricity and gas unit rates and standing charges will remain unchanged until at least the end of this year. ESB's results statement shows that the company continued its significant capital investment in critical energy infrastructure over the first six months of 2026, with almost €1.5 billion invested in capital projects, an increase of over €200m on the same time last year.

stories.title: States must work together to address climate action - EU
stories.summary: European Parliament President Roberta Metsola has called on EU member states to come together to address the climate action crisis in honour of fire fighters, medics and first responders who died fighting wildfires this summer. Speaking in her opening address to MEPs in Strasbourg, France, Ms Metsola said after people "risked their lives to protect others this summer" it is "now up to us, in this House, to work together" to agree new protections "when the next crisis occurs". Ms Metsola, who is one of the most senior figures in the EU, said this summer has seen Europe "once again experience a record breaking series of heat waves". She said during this time "hospital workers fought to protect patients and endured unsafe temperatures at work" and that "brave fire fighters and emergency workers" tried to protect those at risk. The European Parliament's most senior official said the reality is that "this terrible human cost and the combined threat of extreme threat of temperatures and wildfires endangered our communities and damaged our eco-systems, and cost our economies billions". To a round of applause from MEPs, she said while the risk remains clear of the extreme weather events occurring again, the only way to properly honour people whose lives have been lost is for MEPs "to work together" to draw up new climate plans.

stories.title: Littler: I have earned right to take 'crucial days off'
stories.summary: World number one Luke Littler says he has earned the right to pick and choose which tournaments he plays. The 19-year-old has taken a step back this year, limiting the number of lower-key events he has entered as he manages his schedule. Littler has only played two Players Championship floor events, entered just three European Tour tournaments and skipped the recent World Series competitions in New Zealand and Australia. Darts supremo Barry Hearn recently fired a warning to the sport's top stars about regularly missing tournaments, but Littler says he can be his own master given his position at the top of the rankings. He also knows that darts needs him more than he needs darts, with his profile helping drive the sport. "I think obviously it’s just what’s best for me and my family, just having those crucial days off," he said,
